newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Petrol stations hit as French strike hardens.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Petrol stations hit as French strike hardens.

text.p: Petrol stations began to run out of fuel in parts of France on Friday as a blockade by truckers ran into its fifth day and employers warned of lay-offs.
The protests showed the first signs of hurting the economy, although they still fell far short of last year's crippling public transport strikes.

Ignoring calls by Prime Minister Alain Juppe for a quick end to the five-day-old pay strike, truckers set up new blockades around fuel depots, distribution centres and major roads in the provinces in a bid to step up economic pressure.

Economists said economic damage from the strike would probably be shortlived, with senior Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney saying: "If there is an effect it will probably be followed by a rebound."
While the southwest, parts of the south and the Calvados region in Normandy were all badly hit, the majority of shops were working normally and Paris was barely affected.
Petrol stations in southwestern Bordeaux and remote areas of Normandy ran out of fuel and oil companies warned of further shortages if the strike dragged on.
"We can handle the logistics now but if this goes through the weekend we could see stations lacking petrol from Monday," a spokesman for Esso France said.
Oil refineries in the west and at least one plant at the key Mediterranean port of Marseille said truckers had blocked loading bays used to fill road tankers.
Although oil company drivers have not joined the strike, the blockade prevented petrol, diesel and chemicals needed for the plastics industry getting out.

"All the loadings by truck have been halted," said a spokesman for the Shell refinery at Berre near Marseille, adding that usually about one-third of the 15-20,000 tonnes of oil products produced daily left the plant by road in 100 lorries.
He said refineries were still running normally but they may have to adjust if the strikes lasted more than another week.
Supermarket petrol sales rose as more shoppers used a visit to fill their tanks. But there was no sign of panic buying.
Perishable food and farm deliveries were stranded in the Calvados area, a spokeswoman for the local branch of the employers' federation CNPF said.
Distribution firms reported a 50-percent drop in income and several said they were ready to start laying off staff next week, she said.
Supermarkets faced delivery delays but there were no reports of shortages on the shelves, with most holding adequate stocks.
Carmaker Peugeot said it had reduced shifts for two days this week at four of its plants because of a shortage of parts.
Economists said that as was the case with the 1996 public transport strikes, any lost output would be largely offset by higher production when the disruption ended.

"It may reduce consumer spending, there are some problems already with oil, and the same goes for output as much of the traffic in goods is done in trucks," Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro in Paris, said.
"But as was the case last year these effects are always very temporary and I'm not sure they are that big yet, the test being whether Paris gets blocked," Brossard said.
France's economy grew 1.1 percent in the first quarter of this year from the previous strike-hit quarter in which output fell 0.4 percent.
